pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Building a simple circuit

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS2 Year 4 Electricity, statutory):** 'construct a simple series electrical circuit, identifying and naming its basic parts, including cells, wires, bulbs, switches and buzzers.'

- **Standards — US National (NGSS):** no direct grade-3/4 simple-circuit performance expectation; 4-PS3-2 (energy transferred by electric currents) is the nearest strand and is foreshadowed, not met. UK-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children physically assemble a simple series circuit and learn to name its parts (cell/battery, wires, bulb/lamp, switch, buzzer/motor). The learning is a hands-on procedure plus vocabulary, NOT current theory: the win is a circuit that works and the right word for each component. The single most important idea to seed (without theorising) is the COMPLETE LOOP: the bulb only lights when there is an unbroken path from one end of the cell, through the components, back to the other end.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/procedural, age 8-9).
bestPractices: Hands-on first: give real cells, wires, bulbs in holders and crocodile clips and let children build before any diagram — the procedure is learned by doing, and a working bulb is the feedback.
Teach component names as they are used, with the real object in hand, then introduce the conventional circuit symbol only as a label for the thing they've already handled.
Make 'complete loop' the organising idea: have children trace the path with a finger from one terminal of the cell all the way back to the other; if the finger can't get home, the circuit is broken.

Pre-empt the commonest build failures explicitly — bulb not screwed into its holder, crocodile clip on plastic insulation not bare metal, cell the wrong way / flat cell — as a fault-finding checklist.
Confront the 'one wire is enough' idea head-on: many children draw or build a single wire from cell to bulb; show that it will not light and that BOTH terminals must be connected.
keyRepresentations: The real components: cell in a holder, bulb in a holder, wires with crocodile clips, a switch, a buzzer — the canonical Year-4 kit.
The closed-loop diagram drawn as an actual loop (cell → wire → bulb → wire → back to cell), so 'circuit = circle' is visible.
Conventional circuit symbols introduced as name-tags for handled parts (cell, bulb/lamp, switch, buzzer, wire).
A finger-trace overlay: a dotted path the child follows round the loop to check it is complete.
commonMisconceptions: Unipolar / 'one wire' model: a single wire from the battery to the bulb is enough to light it — children ignore the return path.
Clashing-currents model: electricity comes out of BOTH ends of the cell and meets/fights at the bulb to light it.
'The bulb just needs to touch the battery' — not understanding that the path must run through the bulb's two separate contacts.
Confusing 'cell' and 'battery' is fine, but thinking the holder or the wire is the source of power is not — the cell is the source.
Believing more wires or a bigger tangle means more power; circuit topology, not amount of wire, decides whether it lights.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, learners construct a simple series circuit and name its parts (cell/battery, wire, bulb, switch, buzzer), with the central organising idea being the COMPLETE LOOP: a bulb lights only when there is an unbroken path from one terminal of the cell, through the components, back to the other terminal. This is a hands-on procedure plus vocabulary, not current theory. Physical construction with a real kit is the primary aim; a snap-together on-screen builder is a strong companion for topology, vocabulary and procedure rehearsal but does not replace the physical build the curriculum requires.

activities.title: Build the loop with a real kit
feedback: If a single wire from one terminal to the bulb stays dark, prompt: 'Where does the other end go? The current has to get all the way back to the cell's other terminal.'

If a learner thinks electricity comes out of BOTH ends of the cell and meets or 'fights' at the bulb (the clashing-currents idea), trace the single unbroken loop with them: the current runs one way round the whole path, it does not pour out of both terminals to collide at the bulb.

If both bulb wires go to the same terminal or both touch the same point of the bulb, point out the bulb's two separate contacts (tip and side) and the cell's two terminals — each must join the loop at a different point.
When a circuit fails, coach a finger-trace from one terminal all the way round, checking each join, rather than assuming the bulb is broken.
Confirm success by naming what each part does: the cell is the source of power; the wire carries it; the switch opens/closes the loop.
If a learner thinks adding more wire or a bigger tangle gives more power, point out that whether the bulb lights depends on completing the loop, not on the amount of wire.
activities.rationale: The statutory aim is to physically CONSTRUCT a series circuit and name real parts; building by hand with a working bulb as feedback develops both the procedure and the complete-loop intuition. The common unipolar ('one wire is enough') and clashing-currents misconceptions are addressed by emphasising the complete loop and tracing the return path.
sourceClaims: Year 4 statutory requirement to construct a simple series circuit and identify/name cells, wires, bulbs, switches and buzzers.

Unipolar (one-wire) and clashing-currents models are the dominant children's misconceptions when building first circuits; emphasising the complete loop and current the same all the way round are the remedies.
learnerActions: Using real components (cell in a holder, wires with crocodile clips, a bulb in a holder, a switch, a buzzer), build a circuit that lights the bulb or sounds the buzzer.
Name each part out loud as you place it: cell (battery), wire, bulb, switch, buzzer.
Trace the path with your finger starting at one terminal of the cell, through the components, and check it returns to the other terminal.

If it doesn't light, work through a fault-finding checklist: is the bulb screwed into its holder? Is the crocodile clip on bare metal, not plastic insulation? Is the cell flat? Is a wire loose or the switch open?
Once it works, remove one wire, predict what will happen, then check.
activities.intendedInsight: A bulb lights only when the current has a complete, unbroken loop back to the cell; both terminals of the cell and both separate contacts of the bulb must be joined into the loop. Many faults are breaks found by tracing the loop, but a flat cell or blown bulb can leave the bulb dark even when the wires form a loop.

activities.title: Snap-together circuit playground (digital companion)
feedback: When a single wire to one terminal leaves the bulb dark, show the hint 'where does the other end go?'
The 'show the path' overlay confirms a genuinely closed loop; if it cannot complete the circle, the gap is the fault to fix.
Naming on placement reinforces the vocabulary as parts are handled.
If a learner adds extra wires expecting a brighter bulb, note that more wire does not add power — only completing the loop lights the bulb.

If a learner treats the reversed cell as a 'broken' result, clarify that the bulb still lights because reversing does not break the loop; the deliberate failures to compare are the clip on insulation and the flat cell.
activities.rationale: A live-state manipulative lets learners rehearse topology and vocabulary and get self-correcting feedback when the loop opens or closes. The moving-dot path overlay and name-on-placement are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory. This is proposed as a companion to, not a substitute for, the physical kit.
sourceClaims: Unipolar (one-wire) and clashing-currents models are the dominant children's misconceptions when building first circuits; emphasising the complete loop and current the same all the way round are the remedies.
learnerActions: Drag a cell, two wires and a bulb onto a board and click them end to end; watch the bulb glow the instant the loop closes and go dark if any join is pulled apart.
Start by running just ONE wire from the cell to the bulb, notice it stays dark, then add the return wire to the cell's other terminal and see it light.
Read each part's name as it lands ('cell', 'bulb', 'switch', 'buzzer').
Use a 'show the path' toggle that traces the live loop with a moving dot so the unbroken circle is visible.

Explore variations and report what each actually does: a clip on plastic insulation and a flat cell leave the bulb dark, while a reversed single cell still lights it — reversing a cell does not break the loop (a filament bulb is non-polar). Polarity changes behaviour only for a buzzer (which may fall silent reversed) or a motor (which reverses its direction of turn), not for the bulb.
activities.intendedInsight: It is the complete loop — not the bulb merely touching the battery — that lights the bulb; closing or breaking the loop is directly felt through the live bulb state.

activities.title: Name and order the parts (vocabulary & procedure support)
feedback: For symbol-matching, remind learners the symbol is just a label for the object they built with.
For 'which loop lights?', point back to tracing the path: a lit loop is unbroken from terminal to terminal.
Correct 'the holder/wire is the source of power' by reaffirming the cell is the source.
activities.rationale: Tap-to-reveal and matching/sequence/which-loop tasks reinforce the required vocabulary and build sequence. They support recognition of names and order but do not, on their own, elicit the independent physical construction and fault-finding the standard requires, so they belong as support rather than the lead.
sourceClaims: Year 4 statutory requirement to construct a simple series circuit and identify/name cells, wires, bulbs, switches and buzzers.
learnerActions: On a finished circuit, tap each part to reveal its name and what it does (cell, wire, bulb/lamp, switch, buzzer).
Match each conventional circuit symbol to the real part it stands for, introduced as a name-tag for a part already handled.
Put the steps of building a circuit into the correct order.
Choose which of several loops would light (e.g. identify the closed loop versus a broken one).
activities.intendedInsight: Secure the names and jobs of components and the sequence of building, linking symbols to the physical things they label.

constraints: The statutory objective is to physically construct a real series circuit and name real parts; a digital builder or labelled diagram is a companion, not a replacement for the hands-on kit.
Tap-to-reveal diagrams and matching/sequence tasks support vocabulary and procedure recognition but do not, by themselves, elicit independent construction or fault-finding.

This is a procedure-plus-vocabulary objective at age 8–9, NOT current theory: the goals are a working circuit and the correct name for each part, with the complete-loop idea seeded without theorising.
Introduce circuit symbols only after children have handled the real component, as name-tags for things they have already used.
Optional digital features (moving-dot path overlay, name-on-placement, exploring build variations) are illustrative ways to make the loop concrete, not required mechanisms.
Confusing 'cell' and 'battery' is acceptable at this age, but learners should not treat the wire or holder as the source of power — the cell is the source.

A filament bulb is non-polar: a reversed single cell still lights it, so a reversed cell must not be presented as a build failure. Flat cells, clips on insulation, loose or unscrewed bulbs, loose wires, an open switch and a blown bulb are genuine dark-bulb faults; in this kit, polarity can affect only a buzzer (many are polarised) or a motor (direction of turn), not the bulb.
A dialogue/in-role format is not well suited as the lead for this manual build-and-test procedure; the original row rated it poor for developing the build skill.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (IOP Spark misconceptions) was marked verified:false in the row; the misconception remedies it describes should be treated as unconfirmed here.

The original row asserted a 2D board teaches the loop 'better' than 3D and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-preference claims not established by the sources, so they are softened to affordance/limit framing — a 3D or physical bench may add dexterity with real components without teaching the topological loop better.

The original stated a labelled diagram and a quiz 'cannot' deliver the build/loop learning; retained only as the narrower, objective point that recognition/label tasks do not by themselves elicit independent construction.

Physics self-audit: the complete-loop and two-contacts explanations are internally consistent. A flat cell or a clip on plastic insulation leaving the bulb dark, and a reversed single cell still lighting a filament bulb (bulbs are non-polar), are robust outcomes — the reversed cell is a deliberate contrast, not a failure, and is not kit-dependent for a bulb. The original design note's 'reversed cell does nothing' was an error and has been corrected. Polarity affects a buzzer (may silence) and a motor (reverses direction), but does not simply stop those components.

probeDeeper: Trace the path with your finger, starting at the battery — does it come all the way back to the other end?
Your bulb is touching a wire but won't light. How many places does the bulb need to be connected, and where?
It works — now take one wire off. Predict what happens before you look, then check.
What is each part FOR — what does the cell do that the wire doesn't?
assess.correctAnswer: Connects the components in a complete loop — both terminals of the cell joined through the wires, switch and bulb, with the bulb wired into the loop at its two separate contacts — so the bulb lights; names cell, wire, bulb and switch; and when it fails, traces the loop to find the break (loose wire, single connection to the bulb, open switch).

errorPatterns.pattern: One wire is enough — runs a single wire from one battery terminal to the bulb and expects it to light ('electricity flows out to the bulb and that's it') — the unipolar model.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Highlight that the current must RETURN to the other terminal — trace the loop with a finger and connect the second wire.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching — only one connection to the bulb or only one terminal used; the bulb doesn't light and the child doesn't see why.

errorPatterns.pattern: Connects both bulb wires to the same battery terminal, or both to the bottom of the bulb ('as long as it's touching').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the bulb's two separate contacts (tip and side) and the cell's two terminals; each must join the loop at a different point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watching the connection points — no through-loop is formed.

errorPatterns.pattern: When it fails, gives up or swaps the bulb rather than tracing the loop ('the bulb must be broken').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a finger-trace from one terminal all the way round, checking each join — coach the debugging routine rather than reteaching circuits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No systematic loop-tracing when the circuit doesn't work.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a single wire or a single connection (unipolar model), or same-terminal connections; the bulb doesn't light and the loop isn't understood.
responseLevels.full: Builds a complete series loop with the bulb correctly wired at its two contacts, names each component and its role, and diagnoses a broken circuit by tracing the loop for the gap.
responseLevels.partial: Builds a working loop by trial and error and names the parts, but can't reliably trace the complete loop to fix a fault or explain why both connections are needed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a cell, two wires, a bulb and a switch. Build a circuit that lights the bulb. As you go, tell me what each part is — and if it doesn't light, find and fix the problem. [Watch: do they form a complete loop from one terminal of the cell, through the bulb, back to the other terminal, connecting BOTH bulb contacts?]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who builds a genuine loop (two connections, returning to the other terminal) from one who runs a single wire from one terminal to the bulb expecting light (the unipolar/single-wire model) or connects both wires to the same terminal.
